replaySteps.label: Baseline
replaySteps.description: Routine thermal, sulfur dioxide and ground deformation records all sit within the fixture's configured baseline.

replaySteps.label: Thermal observation
replaySteps.description: A thermal anomaly modelled on VIIRS arrives, followed by a MODIS-modelled detection from a later overpass that repeats the same category.

replaySteps.label: Gas observation
replaySteps.description: A sulfur dioxide anomaly modelled on Sentinel-5P TROPOMI adds a second, distinct evidence category.

observations.sourceName: Simulated fixture modelled on Copernicus Sentinel-1 radar interferometry (InSAR)
observations.qualityNote: Simulated value for the demo. InSAR measures change between two acquisitions, not absolute position, and can contain atmospheric artifacts such as water vapour, plus decorrelation on vegetated slopes; a few millimetres is hard to separate from noise.
observations.summary: Line-of-sight ground displacement of 2.5 mm near the summit between two radar acquisitions 12 days apart.

observations.sourceName: Simulated fixture modelled on NASA FIRMS VIIRS 375 m active fire detections
observations.qualityNote: Simulated value for the demo. A satellite hotspot can have non-volcanic causes, such as vegetation fires or hot ground, and needs contextual review; cloud can hide thermal signals, and fire radiative power from one overpass is approximate.
observations.summary: Night-time summit thermal detection with fire radiative power of 2.1 MW.

observations.sourceName: Simulated fixture modelled on Copernicus Sentinel-5P TROPOMI sulfur dioxide (SO2) column
observations.qualityNote: Simulated value for the demo. SO2 retrievals depend on cloud cover and the assumed plume height; values below about 1 DU are close to the detection limit and noisy for a single overpass.
observations.summary: SO2 vertical column of 0.4 Dobson units over the summit area.

observations.sourceName: Simulated fixture modelled on NASA FIRMS VIIRS 375 m active fire detections
observations.qualityNote: Simulated value for the demo. A satellite hotspot can have non-volcanic causes, such as vegetation fires or hot ground, and needs contextual review; cloud can hide thermal signals, and fire radiative power from one overpass is approximate.
observations.summary: Night-time summit hotspot with fire radiative power of 24.6 MW across several 375 m pixels.
observations.anomalyReason: Fire radiative power of 24.6 MW is above the fixture-configured illustrative threshold of 10 MW for this demo; this is not a scientific or official threshold.

observations.sourceName: Simulated fixture modelled on NASA FIRMS MODIS 1 km active fire detections
observations.qualityNote: Simulated value for the demo. MODIS pixels are about 1 km across, so one detection can merge several heat sources; a hotspot can have non-volcanic causes and needs contextual review, and daytime detections are less sensitive and can be cloud-obscured.
observations.summary: Daytime summit hotspot from a later overpass by a second sensor, with fire radiative power of 31.8 MW.
observations.anomalyReason: Fire radiative power of 31.8 MW is above the fixture-configured illustrative threshold of 10 MW for this demo; this is not a scientific or official threshold. It is a second sensor reporting the same thermal category.

observations.sourceName: Simulated fixture modelled on Copernicus Sentinel-5P TROPOMI sulfur dioxide (SO2) column
observations.qualityNote: Simulated value for the demo. SO2 retrievals depend on cloud cover and the assumed plume height; one overpass is a snapshot rather than an emission rate and needs comparison with ground-based gas measurements.
observations.summary: SO2 vertical column of 6.2 Dobson units in a plume drifting west of the summit.
observations.anomalyReason: SO2 column of 6.2 DU is above the fixture-configured illustrative threshold of 2 DU for this demo; this is not a scientific or official threshold.

observations.sourceName: Simulated fixture modelled on NASA FIRMS VIIRS 375 m active fire detections
observations.qualityNote: Simulated value for the demo. A hotspot is not a confirmed fire: land clearing, flaring or hot bare ground can also trigger detections, so it needs contextual review; smouldering peat can burn below detection, and cloud or thick smoke can hide hotspots.
observations.summary: Cluster of daytime thermal detections over drained peatland with combined fire radiative power of 12.4 MW.
observations.anomalyReason: Fire radiative power of 12.4 MW is above the fixture-configured illustrative threshold of 5 MW for this peatland example; this is not a scientific or official threshold.

observations.value: Light smoke haze downwind (north-east) of the hotspot cluster; aerosol signal within the configured baseline for this example.
observations.sourceName: Simulated fixture modelled on Copernicus Sentinel-5P TROPOMI UV aerosol index
observations.qualityNote: Simulated text for the demo. The UV aerosol index indicates absorbing aerosol such as smoke but is sensitive to cloud and plume height; it does not measure ground-level air quality.
observations.summary: Qualitative haze note from an aerosol index review of the area downwind of the hotspots.

observations.value: Standing water limited to paddy fields and river margins near the Chao Phraya and Pa Sak confluence; extent within the seasonal baseline configured for this example.
observations.sourceName: Simulated fixture modelled on a Copernicus Sentinel-1 radar water-extent review
observations.qualityNote: Simulated text for the demo. Radar sees through cloud, but flooded vegetation and built-up areas can hide water and wind-roughened water can be missed; one acquisition shows extent at one moment only.
observations.summary: Qualitative water-extent note from a radar image review; no change beyond the configured seasonal baseline.

observations.sourceName: Simulated fixture modelled on NASA GPM IMERG Early Run satellite precipitation estimate
observations.qualityNote: Simulated value for the demo. Satellite rainfall estimates are grid-cell averages that can under- or over-estimate intense local rain; the Early Run is a near-real-time estimate later superseded by calibrated runs.
observations.summary: Area-average 24-hour rainfall estimate of 38 mm for the period ending at the observation time.
